newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar hovering near 125.50 yen in late Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Dollar hovering near 125.50 yen in late Tokyo.

text.p: The dollar managed to hang on to some of its earlier gains and hovered near 125.50 yen in late Tokyo trade on Wednesday, with further rises curtailed for now by a lack of dollar-buying factors.
Offers by U.S. funds near 125.80 yen, along with exporter sales interest above 126 yen, pushed the greenback lower. But the downside was solid on bargain-hunting, dealers said.
Dealers said there was good buying interest on dips from trading companies, securities firms and life insurers. A dealer with a U.S. bank said there also appeared to be some bids from U.S. banks.

"Since the market tried the downside near 124.80 yen and failed to break through earlier, some operators have decided not to wait for any more dips to that level and are placing bids in the lower 125 yen range," a trust bank dealer said.
But most dealers agreed that if the dollar could not rise to 125.80 yen by the end of Tokyo trade, a further downside try could be possible during European trade.
The dollar fell as low as 124.85 yen during morning trade due to a rise in yields of Japanese government bonds (JGBs).
Stop-loss dollar sales were set off at 125.00 yen but another try to trigger stop-loss selling near 124.80 yen failed.

Mid-morning comments by senior Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara that it would be hard to procure funds for intervention directly from the money market, although later clarified by a different Finance Ministry official, pushed the dollar higher. The market took Sakakibara's remarks as a sign that Japan might not intervene to sell dollars.
But the other MOF official said Japan could use its $220 billion in external reserves promptly if needed.

He added that there are no problems with the current intervention system, in which most of the funds for intervention are procured through the issue of special foreign exchange bills that have been mostly underwritten by the Bank of Japan, and that Sakakibara's remarks meant there would be some problems in the method of raising funds from the market directly without BOJ purchases of bills.
Dealers said the dollar's rise was due more to a need to cover short positions than anything else.

"The situation is merely that they have funds sitting there waiting to be used if necessary for intervention; this is not any kind of big issue. The market was getting a bit short and the comments were a convenient trigger for short-covering," one analyst said.

He added that while he saw the dollar taking aim at technical resistance near 126.30 yen before the end of this week, it was likely to fail. "Probably the dollar will move from 124.60 yen to 126 yen for the rest of this week," he said.
The dollar was down slightly against the mark and dealers said it could dip further during European trade.

Comments on Tuesday by Bundesbank council member Ernst Welteke that he would not welcome further dollar strength were likely to continue to weigh the greenback down on Wednesday, a city bank dealer said, adding that this could also put the dollar under downward pressure against the yen.
